title: vLLM / TensorRT-LLM Engines
summary: Treat the inference engine as a scheduled memory-and-compute system whose configuration must match models, hardware, and service objectives.
overview: Inference engines such as vLLM and TensorRT-LLM implement the runtime beneath model APIs. They manage request scheduling, attention-cache allocation, batching, optimized kernels, and often distributed execution. Their main contribution is efficient execution of supported model workloads, not automatic improvement in model reasoning or application correctness.

Engine capabilities and compatibility vary by release, model architecture, precision, and hardware. A configuration optimized for long offline batches may damage interactive time to first token. Evaluate prefill and decoding separately, account for key-value cache growth, and compare complete service behavior rather than one maximum-throughput benchmark.

production.poc: A prototype serves the actual model and measures realistic prompt and completion distributions on target hardware.
production.production: Production pins engine and driver versions, validates model features, and sets queue, sequence, and memory limits.
production.scale: Enterprise scale manages heterogeneous fleets, distributed placement, engine upgrades, and capacity models grounded in service-level latency and quality constraints.

components.name: API frontend
components.role: Validates requests and translates application settings into supported engine parameters.

components.name: Request scheduler
components.role: Admits and batches prefill and decoding work.

components.name: KV cache manager
components.role: Allocates sequence state and reclaims it on completion or cancellation.

components.name: Execution backend
components.role: Runs compatible kernels across the selected accelerator topology.

components.name: Engine telemetry
components.role: Reports queueing, token throughput, cache pressure, and errors.

flow.title: Validate compatibility
flow.description: Check model architecture, tokenizer, precision, and requested features against the pinned engine release.

flow.title: Profile workload shape
flow.description: Measure input lengths, output lengths, concurrency, and latency targets.

flow.title: Set memory and admission limits
flow.description: Budget weights, cache, activations, and overhead with measured headroom.

flow.title: Schedule generation
flow.description: Allow the engine to batch compatible work while respecting application deadlines.

flow.title: Observe and tune
flow.description: Separate queueing, prefill, decoding, and cancellation behavior before changing parameters.

flow.title: Upgrade by canary
flow.description: Compare outputs and service metrics on a controlled cohort before replacing the fleet.

useCase.title: Serving a document-answering model
useCase.situation: A knowledge assistant serves short questions over contexts of widely varying length.
useCase.problem: A default engine configuration admits too many long prompts and degrades interactive response time.
useCase.requirement: Tune serving capacity around the real mix of prefill and decode work.
useCase.architecture: The team pins an engine release, measures context distributions, and sets token-based admission and cache limits.
runtime: Long-context requests enter a bounded queue instead of exhausting cache.
Telemetry separates prefill delay from decoding speed so tuning targets the actual bottleneck.
useCase.failure: If an engine upgrade changes structured-output behavior or memory use, the canary is rolled back before fleet expansion.
useCase.impact: Measure accepted throughput at the latency objective, not unconstrained tokens per second; a faster benchmark can still produce a worse interactive service.

tradeoffs.cost: Can complicate latency and fairness under mixed workloads.
Consumes cache and increases queueing or per-request latency.

failures.detection: Allocation failures correlate with active sequence tokens.
failures.recovery: Reduce admission and adjust context or concurrency limits.

failures.detection: Tool schemas or sampling settings behave unexpectedly.
failures.recovery: Validate the supported contract and use an evaluated configuration.

mistakes.fix: Tune with the service’s real request distribution.
Optimize accepted throughput under the actual service objective.

whenToUse: Use for self-hosted models at meaningful concurrency.
Use when engine-level scheduling or memory efficiency matters.
Use when hardware-specific optimization justifies operational ownership.
whenNotToUse: Avoid self-hosting solely because an engine exists.
Do not assume feature parity across releases and backends.
Avoid unsupported quantization or model combinations.
checklist: Pin model, engine, driver, and tokenizer.
